edges.description: Loss of the APC sequences C-terminal to the β-catenin regulatory domain disrupts kinetochore-microtubule attachment, a tumour-suppressive function that is separate from Wnt regulation.
Aneuploidy accelerates acquisition of the additional driver mutations that convert adenomas to invasive carcinoma.

Wnt-driven intestinal epithelial adenoma formation produces the hundreds of colonic polyps that define FAP.
APC two-hit progression in FAP adenomas drives colorectal cancer development.

nodes.description: Germline heterozygous APC mutations result in one functional allele. Somatic loss or mutation of the remaining wild-type allele (second hit) eliminates APC function, initiating adenoma formation. This follows Knudson's two-hit hypothesis for tumor suppressor gene inactivation.

evidence.reference_title: Desmoid Tumors in Familial Adenomatous Polyposis.
evidence.snippet: In agreement with Knudson's 'two-hit' theory, the inactivation of the residual APC gene in FAP is a critical step in the development of both colorectal cancer and desmoids.

nodes.description: APC accumulates at the kinetochore during mitosis and is required for efficient microtubule attachment. Truncating alleles that remove the APC sequences C-terminal to the β-catenin regulatory domain produce chromosome and spindle aberrations, so APC loss drives aneuploidy through a route that does not pass through β-catenin. This parallel arm is thought to accelerate the accumulation of the additional driver lesions required for adenomas to become carcinomas, and it is the reason Wnt-directed intervention alone may not capture the whole consequence of APC loss.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in the APC tumour suppressor gene cause chromosomal instability.
evidence.snippet: Here we show that Apc mutant ES cells display extensive chromosome and spindle aberrations, providing genetic evidence for a role of APC in chromosome segregation.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in the APC tumour suppressor gene cause chromosomal instability.
evidence.snippet: Apc mutant cells form mitotic spindles with an abundance of microtubules that inefficiently connect with kinetochores.

nodes.description: Sustained Wnt pathway activation drives adenoma development. Adenomas are benign neoplasms but represent the first step in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence. In FAP, hundreds to thousands of adenomas develop, dramatically increasing the probability that one will progress to carcinoma.

evidence.reference_title: Desmoid Tumors in Familial Adenomatous Polyposis.
evidence.snippet: It is characterized by the presence of hundreds of colonic polyps, which have a high tendency to undergo malignant transformation.

nodes.description: Without prophylactic surgery, colorectal cancer develops in nearly 100% of patients with classic FAP, typically by age 40. The average age of cancer diagnosis is 39 years without surveillance/intervention. The age at which risk rises is genotype dependent rather than uniform: in a genetically confirmed Japanese registry cohort the risk of stage II-IV colorectal cancer rose sharply at about age 34 in patients whose variant lay outside the attenuated-FAP-associated regions and only at about age 49 in those whose variant lay inside them.

nodes.description: Nuclear β-catenin activates TCF/LEF transcription factors, driving expression of Wnt target genes including MYC, CCND1 (cyclin D1), and others that promote cell cycle progression. This results in uncontrolled proliferation of intestinal crypt cells, forming adenomatous polyps.

APC normally functions in the destruction complex (with Axin, GSK3β, CK1) to phosphorylate β-catenin, targeting it for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Loss of APC allows β-catenin to accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and activate Wnt target genes driving proliferation.
